Review: a $300 robot vacuum that maps your whole kitchen

Published 2026-10-06 02:30 UTC

The latest budget robot vacuum we tested costs $300 and offers lidar mapping that would have been reserved for $800 models a few years ago. Within one cleaning run, it produced an accurate floor plan of our test home, identified the kitchen, living room and hallway on its own, and let us draw no-go zones around a pet bowl and a tangle of charging cables.

Navigation was the highlight. The vacuum moved in neat parallel lines, rarely bumped into furniture, and returned to its dock reliably when the battery ran low. It recognized when we moved a chair and updated the map rather than getting confused. Scheduling cleaning for individual rooms worked well, and the vacuum remembered which rooms needed more passes.

Suction was the weak point. The vacuum picked up crumbs and dust on hard floors easily, but it struggled with sand ground into a low-pile rug and left behind cat hair along baseboards. A single side brush means corners get less attention than on pricier models with two brushes. The bin is small and needed emptying after every full clean.

The companion app was our biggest frustration. During setup, it asked for location access, contact lists and permission to scan for nearby devices on the network. Only location is needed to finish the Wi-Fi setup, and the app kept working after we denied the rest. Its privacy policy says map data may be used to improve products, and the option to opt out is buried three menus deep.

Battery life was about 110 minutes on the standard power setting, which was enough to clean our 1,200-square-foot test home in one go. The mopping attachment is basic: it drags a damp pad behind the vacuum and cannot lift itself on carpet, so you have to remove it before cleaning rugs.

Overall, the mapping is impressive for the price, but buyers with pets or lots of carpet should spend more on a model with stronger suction and a self-emptying dock.
